summary: Concurrent retries causing out-of-order tool/function executions across Python + Go SDKs
summary_long: Customer observed that when two backend services (one using Python SDK, one using Go SDK) concurrently call the same conversation with function/tool invocations and experience transient 429s, the final sequence of tool executions can become re-ordered. This leads to state inconsistencies (e.g., 'confirm' processed before 'debit').
description:
Issue summary:
Customers (FinScale Labs) reported a reproducible scenario where concurrent clients using different Redwood SDKs trigger retries and the order of function/tool executions does not match the original logical ordering in the prompt. This is producing application-level data inconsistencies for financial flows.
impact: Customer encountering incorrect ordering for multi-step function sequences (debit -> confirm). Affected production jobs process ~500 requests/min; ~1 in 400 requests show reorder symptoms after retry storms, causing reconciliation failures and manual intervention.
steps_to_reproduce: 1) Setup shared conversation id between two services: Service A (Python SDK) and Service B (Go SDK).
2) Service A sends a request that triggers function call 'debit_account' then returns streaming tokens.
3) Concurrently, Service B sends a followup request referencing same convo that triggers 'confirm_debit'.
4) Induce transient 429s at api-gateway (rate limit burst) or drop streaming connection to force client-side retries with exponential backoff.
5) Observe on the backend logs that retry attempts from different SDKs arrive close in time and are routed to different serving instances.
6) Verify final order of tool invocations in audit logs (found confirm before debit in failing traces).
expected_behavior: Retries and concurrent requests that target the same logical conversation should preserve the logical ordering of tool/function invocations, or at minimum support deterministic at-most-once semantics when idempotency is used.
actual_behavior: In failing traces, 'confirm_debit' executes prior to 'debit_account' because a retried/late message from Service A was processed after Service B's request. The SDK-level and gateway retries appear correlated with request routing to different serving nodes and non-deterministic merging of queued tool calls.
logs: TraceID: trc-20260310-91a2 - Service A (py-sdk) initial request -> request_id=R-1132 attempt=0 routed-> node-srv-07
TraceID: trc-20260310-91a2 - Service B (go-sdk) concurrent request -> request_id=R-1140 attempt=0 routed-> node-srv-12
TraceID: trc-20260310-91a2 - api-gateway returned 429 to R-1132 at 2026-03-10T14:22:03Z, client retried attempt=1 -> routed-> node-srv-12 at 2026-03-10T14:22:04Z
Audit: tool-call debit_account request_id=R-1132 processed at node-srv-12 at 2026-03-10T14:22:05Z (late), confirm_debit request_id=R-1140 processed at node-srv-12 at 2026-03-10T14:22:04Z
Observed that node-srv-12 executed confirm_debit before processing the retried debit_account message; sequence_token logs show missing sequence gap for conversation-id conv-5582.
investigation_notes: Initial triage: reproduced in staging by simulating 429 bursts via gateway throttle. Failure only reproduced when two different SDK clients sent near-simultaneous requests referencing same conversation-id.
Checked SDK versions: python 1.4.2, go 0.9.7 - both use client-side retry but differ slightly in jitter backoff and header ordering.
Routing logs show retried messages can land on different serving nodes and are enqueued for per-conversation processing; node-local dequeues respect arrival order per node, not global logical time.
Sequence token implementation relies on per-node in-memory ordering when multiplexed; gap emerges when late retry arrives to a node that already processed a later logical message from another node.
hypothesis: Race condition between inter-node routing and per-node queue ordering: retries arriving at a node after a later message from another node result in out-of-order execution because global sequencing is not enforced at ingest time.
SDK differences (jitter/backoff and header normalization) increase the likelihood of cross-node routing for retries; absence of a conversation-level global sequence gate allows reorder.
Idempotency keys are present but scoped to entire request not to discrete tool invocations, so they do not guarantee ordering when separate calls reference the same conversation id.
workaround: Short-term: Advise customer to serialize critical multi-step flows via a single client (stick to a single SDK instance for ordering-sensitive sequences).
Use explicit per-action idempotency tokens in metadata for each tool call (e.g., X-Idempotency-Action) so server can dedupe and enforce application-level ordering checks in customer logic.
Temporarily increase retry-backoff jitter or centralize retries into an orchestrator process to avoid cross-node arrival races.
next_steps: SRE/Runtime: evaluate adding conversation-level ingest gating or a global sequence coordinator for ordering-sensitive conversations.
SDK Team: add guidance and helper utilities for per-action idempotency tokens and provide a best-practice pattern in SDK docs for ordering-critical flows.
Support: work with FinScale Labs to roll out the temporary orchestrator approach and monitor for reduction in reorders.
